description_ru: В последний день работы часовой мастерской в неё заходит женщина с исправными часами, которые просто остановились. Мастер понимает, что чинить нужно не механизм.
text:
On the last day before the shop closed for good, Anselm Duret sold nothing, repaired nothing, and answered the telephone only once, to tell a salesman that he was already retired in every sense that mattered. The building had been sold to a company that intended to turn it into a juice bar. He had received the news with his customary stoicism, which is to say that he had gone quiet for a week and then bought an expensive pair of shoes.

Duret and Daughter had stood on the corner of Rue des Tanneurs for sixty-three years. The daughter was long gone, to Montreal and then to a series of other lives, but the sign remained, and so did the clocks. Hundreds of them hung in the window and along the walls, every one of them set to a slightly different minute, so that at any hour the shop seemed to be quietly arguing with itself. Customers used to say that it was impossible to be late there, since whatever time you arrived, some clock was always willing to agree with you. Duret had considered this the finest compliment the establishment ever received.

At ten to five, the doorbell chimed. A woman in a grey raincoat came in, shaking water from an umbrella. She might have been forty or sixty; there was something about her face that refused to commit. In her hand she held a small wristwatch with a cracked glass and a strap worn pale at the buckle. "I'm afraid we're closing," said Duret. "Permanently, in fact. Today." "Then I'm in time," she said, and set the watch on the counter. "It stopped last Thursday. I'd like it to start again, if that's not too much trouble."

He sighed, because courtesy had been trained into him so thoroughly that it survived even despair, and fitted his loupe into his eye. The movement was a Swiss calibre from the nineteen-fifties, plain and honest, the sort of mechanism built by people who expected it to outlive them. He opened the case back. The balance wheel was perfect. The mainspring was fine. Every jewel and every tooth was exactly where it ought to be.

"There's nothing wrong with it," he said. "I know." He looked up. She was gazing at the wall of clocks with an expression he could not quite read, fond and guilty at once, like someone watching a house she used to live in.

"It was my father's," she said. "He wore it every day, for forty years. When he died, I put it in a drawer, because I couldn't bear the ticking. It seemed so cheerful about it, so absolutely uninterrupted. Last week I took it out and wound it, and it ran for three days, and then it stopped, and I haven't been able to think about anything else." She smiled, with some effort. "I thought perhaps you could tell me why."

Duret was not a sentimental man. In sixty years he had learned that most stopped watches had perfectly mundane explanations, dust, a dried drop of oil, a customer who had dropped them on a tiled floor and was ashamed to say so. He examined this one for a long time, turning it under the lamp, while a hundred clocks around them ticked out their disagreement, and the rain tapped at the window like an impatient customer who had somewhere else to be. Eventually he found the cause, and it was not a defect.

"Madame," he said. "Look here." He pointed with a tweezer to a tiny worn patch on the winding crown. "This has been turned the same number of times every morning for four decades, always at roughly the same hour, always by the same hand. The metal remembers. The watch is accustomed to being wound by someone who loves it. It stopped because it was waiting." She stared at him. "That's absurd." "It is completely absurd," he agreed. "I am a craftsman, not a poet. But I have had this mechanism open on my bench for ten minutes, and I assure you that the only thing wrong with it is that it has not yet been told." "Told what?" "I don't know. Whatever you need to say to it." He pushed the watch gently across the counter. "Wind it yourself, every morning, for a month. If it still stops, bring it back to whoever takes over this shop, and I will personally haunt him."

The woman laughed, and then, to her evident surprise, she wept, briefly and without drama, as if a window had been opened in a stuffy room. Duret found a clean handkerchief and a chair, and the two of them sat in the dusk for some time without saying anything much, while the clocks went on disagreeing around them.

When she left, he did not turn the sign to Closed immediately. Instead he walked down the shop, from clock to clock, winding each of them for the last time, an old, deliberate ritual. At the grandfather clock by the door, which had stopped in 1994 and which no customer had ever asked him to repair, he paused. Then he opened the glass case, reached in, and gave the key a single, gentle turn.

For a moment, nothing. Then a soft, wooden tick, hesitant as a first word after a long silence, and then another, and then a steady, patient rhythm that filled the quiet shop like warm water. Duret smiled. The juice bar, he thought, was going to have a very peculiar atmosphere.

focus_sounds.tip_ru: Ударение: ˈcustomary, sentiˈmental, acˈcustomed. Не путайте: ударение в customary на первый слог.
Звук «ʌ» короткий и открытый, как нечто среднее между «а» и «ъ»: customary, stuffy.
В конце слов hand, wound, closed не оглушайте «d»: звук должен быть звонким.

questions.question: Why was Duret's shop closing?
questions.answer: The building was sold to become a juice bar.

questions.question: What was wrong with the woman's watch?
questions.answer: Nothing was mechanically wrong; it had stopped as if waiting to be wound by her father.

questions.question: What did Duret advise her to do?
questions.answer: To wind it herself every morning for a month.

questions.question: What did he do before he left?
questions.answer: He wound all the clocks, including the grandfather clock that had stopped in 1994.
